name: NPL caesium atomic clock
description: Louis Essen and J. V. L. Parry built a caesium atomic clock at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, using an atomic transition as a timekeeping reference.

date.label: May 1955
date.basis: NIST dates the unveiling to May 1955; the museum attributes the 1955 clock to Essen and Parry.

events.statement: The NPL caesium clock built by Essen and Parry was unveiled in May 1955.

evidence.supports: Identifies Essen, Parry, NPL, Teddington and 1955.
Dates the unveiling to May 1955 and describes earlier research and the Ramsey design.
Attributes the device to J. V. L. Parry.

earliest_record.rationale: The inspected evidence establishes the May 1955 unveiling, not the first conception or universal first atomic clock.

measures.subject: The 1955 NPL caesium clock
measures.conditions: Museum retrospective gives an equivalent rate; it does not report a 300-year observation or specify the measurement interval.

evidence.supports: Reports accuracy equivalent to one second in 300 years.

caveats: NIST describes an earlier ammonia-based atomic clock; the present record is the specific NPL caesium apparatus, not a global first claim. Later SI definition did not require adoption of this one device.

missing_prerequisites: Ramsey’s 1949 separated-oscillatory-field measurement design used in the caesium clock.

unresolved.note: NIST identifies the 1949 design in this clock, but a separate record and the original design publication remain to be examined before a directed link is added.

evidence.supports: States that Essen used a design invented by Norman Ramsey in 1949.

research.note: Independent parent checked SMG object1962-59 and NIST historical sections. Performance remains a catalogue claim; NPL is host rather than an inferred separate developer or funder.

organizations.note: Laboratory where the instrument was built; funding not inferred.
